The writer's own hand
Blessing and farewell
Opening: sender, readers, greeting

An ancient letter began with one formula: the sender's name, the reader's name, and a greeting. "Apion to Epimachus his father and lord, many greetings," wrote a young Egyptian soldier in the second century. James and the Jerusalem letter in Acts keep the plain Greek word for "greeting" (chairein); Paul and Peter enlarge every part, naming the sender's calling and describing the readers, and turn the greeting into a blessing: "Grace to you and peace." The address itself, Deissmann notes, was written on the outside of the folded sheet, and none of the New Testament letters preserves it. Acts 15:23 James 1:1 Romans 1:7 [1][11][5]

LETTERS ABOUT LETTERS
Letters that mention letters
Where one letter speaks of another, including letters now lost.

2 Peter → Paul's letters · "All his epistles" 2 Peter calls Paul "our beloved brother", knows "all his epistles", finds "some things hard to be understood" in them, and sets them beside "the other scriptures". It is the only place where one group of letters speaks of another, and the earliest hint of Paul's letters read as a set; how early depends on the date of 2 Peter, which is disputed (Zahn about 60-63, Chase about 150). 2 Peter 3:15–16 [20][14]

2 Peter → 1 Peter · "This second epistle" "This second epistle, beloved, I now write unto you." Read most simply, the first is 1 Peter. Zahn, as Bigg reports, thought it an earlier letter now lost; Mayor held that 2 Peter was not sent to the readers of 1 Peter at all. 2 Peter 3:1 [20][22]

Colossians → The letter from Laodicea · Exchange letters Paul tells Colossae to have its letter read at Laodicea and to "read the epistle from Laodicea". Lightfoot sorts the old answers: a letter the Laodiceans wrote; a letter written from Laodicea (1 Timothy, say); or a letter to Laodicea, lost, or forged later, or Ephesians sent round as a circular, which was his own view. The Muratorian list already rejects a forged letter "to the Laodiceans". Colossians 4:16 [9][35]

1 Corinthians → An earlier letter to Corinth · "I wrote unto you in an epistle" "I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators": a letter before 1 Corinthians, now lost. Shaw (ISBE) suggests that 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1 may preserve "a stray fragment" of it. 1 Corinthians 5:9 2 Corinthians 6:14–7:1 [15][16]

Corinth's letter → 1 Corinthians · "The things whereof ye wrote unto me" The traffic ran both ways: the Corinthians had written to Paul, and 1 Corinthians answers them, taking up topic after topic with "Now concerning". Shaw thinks Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus brought the church's letter. 1 Corinthians 7:1 1 Corinthians 7:25 1 Corinthians 8:1 1 Corinthians 12:1 1 Corinthians 16:17 [15]

2 Corinthians → The tearful letter · "With many tears" Paul recalls a letter written "out of much affliction and anguish of heart ... with many tears" that made them sorry. Easton took it to be 1 Corinthians; Shaw (ISBE) treats it as a separate "severe letter", and reports the view, from Hausrath (1870) on, that it survives as 2 Corinthians 10-13. 2 Corinthians 2:3–4 2 Corinthians 7:8 [19][16]

2 Corinthians → Paul's letters · "Weighty and powerful" Paul quotes what his critics said of his letters: "weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak". Schaff counts this among the signs that Paul wrote more letters than survive. 2 Corinthians 10:9–11 [5]

2 Corinthians → Letters of commendation · "Epistles of commendation" "Need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you?" Letters introducing a traveller were common; Deissmann prints papyrus examples and points to Romans 16, which opens "I commend unto you Phebe", as Paul's own use of the form. 2 Corinthians 3:1–2 Romans 16:1 1 Corinthians 16:3 [1]

2 Thessalonians → A forged letter · "Nor by letter as from us" The Thessalonians were not to be shaken "by letter as from us", which may mean a forged letter or a misreading of a real one; the verse does not say which. The letter closes with Paul's own hand as "the token in every epistle", a safeguard Lightfoot connects with such forgeries. 2 Thessalonians 2:2 2 Thessalonians 3:17 [8][1]

2 Thessalonians → 1 Thessalonians · "Our epistle" "Hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle": 2 Thessalonians points back to a letter the church already had. The only earlier letter of Paul to Thessalonica that survives is 1 Thessalonians, and Easton reads the second letter as correcting a misunderstanding of the first. 2 Thessalonians 2:15 [19]

Ephesians → An earlier writing · "As I wrote afore in few words" "As I wrote afore in few words": Schaff and Pratt (ISBE) count this among the traces of letters that have not survived. The verse itself does not say whether it means another letter or the earlier part of Ephesians. Ephesians 3:3 [5][11]

3 John → A letter to the church · "I wrote unto the church" The elder had written to Gaius's church, but Diotrephes "receiveth us not". Zahn, Schmiedel and Findlay identified that letter with 2 John; Harnack, Brooke and Law (ISBE) did not, since the two letters face different problems. 3 John 1:9 [18][26]

1 John → "I have written" · "I write ... I have written" 1 John says "I write unto you" four times and then "I have written unto you" twice (the Revised Version reads three and three). Plummer lists seven explanations: the second refers to the Gospel of John, which he thought most likely; to a lost earlier letter, for which "we have no evidence whatever"; to the first part of 1 John; and others, including the letter-writer's habit of looking at the letter from the reader's side. 1 John 2:12–14 [25]

Jude → A letter Jude meant to write · "Of the common salvation" Jude had set out to write "of the common salvation" but found it "needful" to write instead an appeal to "contend for the faith": a glimpse of one letter put aside for another. Jude 1:3
